pronunciation.approximation: Say "viracocha" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Wiraqucha".

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: wira 'fat, grease, foam' + qucha 'lake, sea' — the gloss 'lake of fat' is the chroniclers' own (Murúa, Historia general del Piru)

kin.label: Aymara
kin.form: Wilaquta, 'red lake' — the Aymara form of the name, still spoken around Lake Titicaca

kin.label: Epithets
kin.form: Ticci, 'foundation, beginning,' and Pachayachachic, 'creator of the world' (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica)

pronunciation.note: Wiraqucha is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the restored form is plain ASCII, with no distinctive feature the ASCII alphabet loses. The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, grease, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea' — Father Murúa glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.' The restoration follows modern Quechua orthography rather than the colonial Spanish spelling Viracocha.

domains.title: Wiraqucha
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Wiraqucha is the maker of the Inca cosmos: sky father, creator of sun and moon, and the weeping wanderer who once walked the length of the Andes and was never seen again. The chroniclers knew him as the invisible god who made the world and then withdrew from it — and his name still survives in the politest word an Andean elder can offer a stranger: wiraqucha, sir, gentleman, lord.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea'; the chroniclers glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.'

cards.name: Creator
cards.desc: Maker of the sun, moon, and stars and of every nation; to the Andes he is Pachayachachic, 'creator of the world.'

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Honored at Titicaca, Tiwanaku, and Cusco; his cult outlived the empire and endures in solstice pilgrimage, shrine, and everyday address.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple; the scholarly restoration Wiraqucha replaces the colonial spelling Viracocha with modern Quechua orthography.

symbols.name: Sea foam of the lake
symbols.meaning: The etymon wira-qucha, 'foam (or fat) of the lake' — the foam from which the name, and the god, emerged

symbols.name: The staff and traveler's bundle
symbols.meaning: He crossed the Andes as a staff-carrying beggar, weeping at springs and prophesying — the god as itinerant stranger

symbols.name: The reed float
symbols.meaning: The totora-reed float that bore the two survivors of the flood — the seed of the remade world

symbols.name: The stone models of Tiwanaku
symbols.meaning: The sculpted prototypes of every nation, from which Wiraqucha shaped humankind at his workshop

symbols.name: The golden image of Cusco
symbols.meaning: The solid-gold statue in the Coricancha, described by Cobo and Murúa and melted down within years of the conquest

mythology.lead: Wiraqucha's mythology reaches us only through the reports of conquered lords to Spanish chroniclers — Betanzos, Cobo, Sarmiento — yet it holds together a coherent cosmic biography: the making of the world, the flood that erased its first people, the shaping of the nations at Tiwanaku, and a final journey westward that ended in disappearance.

myths.title: The Flood of Unu Pachakuti
myths.text: Juan de Betanzos, whose Suma y Narración de los Incas (1551) is the fullest early account, tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without worship, so he resolved to undo them. He sent a great flood — unu pachakuti, a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose into the sky above Titicaca. Yet he spared two, a man and a woman, calling them from the waters onto a float of totora reeds near the island, and commissioning them as the ancestors of a new humanity. The myth fixes the shape of Andean time: catastrophe and renewal in cycles, a world unmade and remade, with the creator always watching from above. It is also a charter for the lake itself — Titicaca is not scenery but the hinge where the first world ended and the second began.

myths.title: The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku
myths.text: Father Bernabé Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each with its own face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life. When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find their homelands: one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco. Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Indica (ch. 6–7) gives the same program and adds the full titulature: Ticci Uiracocha Pachayachachic, 'ancient foundation, creator of the world.' The myth is a map of the Andes read backward — every people is the deliberate work of the same hand, and the Inca are simply the nation that remembered best who made them.

myths.title: The Sun, Moon, and Stars
myths.text: The same accounts make Wiraqucha the maker of the sky. On the island of Titicaca in the great lake he fashioned the Sun — Inti — and the Moon, and set the stars in their courses, appointing the Sun the most honored of all, 'like a rich ornament' among the rest (Sarmiento de Gamboa, ch. 7; Cobo 13.3). In imperial theology Inti then became the visible ancestor of the Inca dynasties, while Wiraqucha remained the invisible maker behind the visible god — a two-tier heaven in which the sun was, as it were, the son, and the emperor the sun's line. The pairing let Cusco worship a present, national god without ever forgetting the older, unbounded one above and behind him. It is one of the few world mythologies in which the supreme creator deliberately steps back from the machinery of daily rule, delegating the visible sky to his own workmanship and reserving for himself only the authorship of everything.

myths.title: The Weeping Stranger
myths.text: Betanzos closes the biography with Wiraqucha's departure. The maker walked the length of the Andes in the dress of a poor traveler, staff in hand, teaching as he went and weeping at springs; in the province of the Canchis he wept, foretelling that men dressed exactly as he was — bearded strangers from across the sea — would one day come and overturn the land. He came as far as the region of Manta on the coast and then, Betanzos says, passed into the sea and was gone. The detail is breathtaking in hindsight: a colonial-era text, written within twenty years of Pizarro, preserving a native prophecy that fits the conquest like a glove — and whatever its origin, the story made Wiraqucha the god who knew the strangers before they arrived. A maker who weeps over the future of his own work is a rare figure in any pantheon; the Andes kept him.

lore.syncretism: Spanish missionaries moved quickly to identify Wiraqucha with the Christian God: Father Bernabé Cobo reports Andean lords hearing the gospel and concluding that this Dios must be their own Pachayachachic, finally named. The identification stuck — in Andean parishes 'Dios Pachayachachic' is still a natural sentence — and it let the old shrine centers be absorbed rather than erased, most completely at Copacabana on Titicaca's shore, where the basilica of the Virgin stands where pilgrims once took ship for the island shrines. More remarkably, the god's name became a title for the conquerors themselves: from the earliest chronicles onward, viracocha meant a Spaniard, a gentleman, a lord — the word a conquered people used for strangers who arrived dressed, as Betanzos' prophecy said, exactly like their departing god. Even Tiwanaku's sculpted Gateway of the Sun is popularly read as his image, though that identification is a modern antiquarian conjecture — the gate predates the name by centuries.
lore.culturalLegacy: Wiraqucha never lost his mountain. Pilgrims still cross to the Island of the Sun and Moon on Titicaca, and each June solstice thousands gather at Tiwanaku to watch the sun rise through the Gate of the Sun — a rite older than any written version of the myth it now frames. In modern Quechua and Aymara, wiraqucha remains an honorific — sir, elder, gentleman — a fragment of the god carried in everyday address. The modern Inti Raymi festival at Sacsayhuamán keeps the creator in public view, and the story of the weeping god who foresaw the bearded strangers is still told as the Andes' own prophecy of the conquest. The empire that carried his name fell in a generation; the name outlived the empire by five centuries and is still a polite word for a stranger on a mountain road.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Wiraqucha is the absent creator — the maker who finished his work, wept once over what was coming, and left. Andean theology has no jealous guardian and no returning savior: the world was handed over, and what happens in it is, up to a point, the world's own business. That withdrawal is the deepest note in his mythology. Where other high gods demand attention, Wiraqucha demands only remembrance — his name spoken in honorifics, his lake crossed at the solstice, his ruined workshop kept as pilgrimage ground.

And the weeping is the detail that keeps scholars returning. A god who cries at a spring, foretelling bearded men in his own dress, is a god who has read the ending of the story he began. The chronicles that preserve the scene were written under colonial rule, which should make us careful — but even as colonial construction it is extraordinary: a conquered people explaining the conquest in the voice of their own god, who saw it coming and left before it arrived. Absence, prophecy, grief: the maker's last gifts were the ones no one could take.

lore.archaeology: Wiraqucha's archaeology is the archaeology of his stage. Tiwanaku, the great center of the altiplano (c. 500–1000 CE), holds the Kalasasaya platform, the monumental Gateway of the Sun, and the precision-cut blocks of Puma Punku — the ruins later tradition named as his workshop, where the myth says he modeled the nations in stone. On the Island of the Sun and Island of the Moon in Lake Titicaca, Inca pilgrims' shrines — the Chincana labyrinths, the sacred rock, the sanctuary terraces — mark the myth's exact geography, and Copacabana's basilica stands on the shore where the ritual boats once left. In Cusco, the chroniclers describe a solid-gold image of the god in the Coricancha (Cobo; Murúa), melted down within years of 1532. No pre-Columbian inscription names him: the ruins give the stage, and the chronicles give the script.
